source.title: Training-Free Robot Pose Estimation using Off-the-Shelf Foundational Models

record.tranche_reason: Extends the question of downstream performance scaling to vision-language models estimating robot-arm poses. It measures task error at different reasoning-token budgets and parameter sizes, but does not measure language-model pretraining loss or the original scaling laws.
record.gate_note: The study reports robot-pose errors for frontier models and scaling conditions. Only the reasoning-token and parameter-size comparisons bear on downstream performance versus scale (V6). Other reported model/subset results do not test the listed scaling claims.
record.test_reason: Its Table 3 compares two Qwen3-VL thinking sizes (30B, 235B) on one downstream task, robot-arm pose estimation. That bears weakly on V6 in a new setting. The reasoning-token comparison is test-time compute, not the model scale V6 names.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly correct. Frontier VLMs can estimate approximate robot-arm poses but not precise joint angles. Test-time scaling and parameter scaling alone are insufficient for better estimates. The authors also conclude that VLMs struggle to calibrate their uncertainty bounds. They explicitly do not claim that larger size worsens performance.
record.recipe_differences: Uses reference-target prompting and pose-error evaluation on vision-language models, rather than fitting held-out pretraining-loss curves or studying compute-optimal training allocations.
record.method_sensitivity: The tested reasoning-token budgets and parameter sizes did not produce consistent improvement; the paper describes camera field of view and pose constraints as possible sources of joint-specific error differences.

fits_no_version.finding: Raising Sonnet-4.5's reasoning-token budget from 1,000 to 5,000 or 10,000 gives no significant change in pose error (0.416, 0.392, 0.405).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Downstream task performance improves with test-time (reasoning-token) compute.

record.problems: The authors note that DREAM-Mini is small and uses only one robot-arm type. The scaling comparisons cover limited models and settings; no statistical uncertainty estimates are reported.
record.rows_left_out: No results bearing on the listed scaling versions were left out.

untested.parts: Performance as a function of pretraining loss. Any scaling trend beyond two model sizes. Downstream tasks other than Panda-arm pose estimation. Subsets other than Orb for the size comparison.

record.verdict_notes: The 235B model's 'within bound' rate improved (16.67% vs 5.80%), but its average error, the main metric, worsened. Single-author preprint with a small dataset; the scaling results are described as preliminary. The study cites Kaplan et al. only to motivate the parameter-scaling comparison.

versions.untested_parts: No held-out language-model pretraining loss is measured against parameters, tokens, or compute.
No small-run fit is used to predict larger-run loss.
No fixed-compute allocation between parameters and training tokens is tested.
No comparison of architecture details at fixed parameter count is made.
The study uses vision-language models for a robotics task, but does not test whether power-law loss scaling holds in other modalities or training regimes.
Tests task error for robot-pose estimation against reasoning-token budget and parameter size; does not test performance against pretraining loss or other downstream tasks.
No fitting choices, exponents, compute-optimal allocation, or bending of fitted loss curves are examined.

rows.subject: qwen-3-vl
rows.operation_detail: Compared parameter sizes for pose estimation.
rows.note: The larger model has higher average error; the authors state that parameter scaling alone was not sufficient for reliable pose estimates.
rows.check: Average error rises from 0.395 (30B) to 0.553 (235B). Only two models, 49 images, one task, no uncertainty. The authors caution this does not imply an inverse size–performance correlation.

relationships.condition: Qwen3-VL thinking 30B vs 235B, Orb view subset of DREAM-Mini (49 images), average joint-angle error
relationships.reason: R5: the larger model has higher error (0.553 vs 0.395 at 30B, R4). This is weak evidence: two points, one task, no uncertainty, and the authors call the size scaling insufficient rather than inverse.
relationships.display_finding: Average joint-angle error rose from 0.395 at 30B to 0.553 at 235B, based on two models and 49 images without reported uncertainty.
